cases.name: Bertha Jean Mason
cases.about: Her friend Carolyn Billups said Bertha loved to dance and sing and had a lyrical laugh that drew people to her. "Bertha thought she was Aretha Franklin, " said Billups. Bertha's mother worked long hours which left her to cook and clean and look after her brother and sister. Her aunt Bernice Brookins was frustrated by the lack of police progress and wonders if there would have been more urgency of Bertha had not been a drug user or had been a white woman from the suburbs. She said Bertha was more than just some crack head and that she had another life and people who loved and cared for her.

cases.name: Lisa Moffett-Wiens
cases.about:
Brenda Moffett says her 40-year-old daughter was a trusting person who had struggled with addiction.

"She would struggle to get back to doing what she needed to do to get well. She was in the process of doing that again when this happened. And time just ran out," Brenda Moffett said. 

Lisa Moffett-Wiens, a caring and loving individual, fell victim to a senseless act of violence. Overcoming personal struggles, Lisa was on a journey to leave her addiction behind and create a better life for herself. Lisa's mother, Brenda Moffett, tearfully described her daughter as someone with a big heart and urged others not to remember her solely for the circumstances of her death. Brenda Moffett wants her daughter to be remembered for the person she was—a caring and loving individual. Lisa's struggles with addiction should not overshadow her genuine nature and the efforts she made to overcome her challenges. Brenda emphasizes that no one deserves to be a victim of such heinous acts and hopes that Lisa's memory will be honored by celebrating her kind-hearted spirit.

cases.name: Brittanie St. Ann
cases.about:
She worked at various times as a teacher, nursing assistant and truck driver. "Bubbly, goofy and outspoken" is how her mother described St. Ann, who was born in New Orleans in 1990 and raised in the 7th Ward.

The oldest of six siblings, she moved between New Orleans, Detroit and Austin, before ultimately getting her GED from the Jefferson Parish school system in 2007.

She earned certification as a nursing assistant and worked as a home health aid, followed by a stint as a teaching assistant for special needs children at Walter G. Schneckenburger Elementary School in Kenner. Then she hit the road as a semi-truck driver.

"She loved the fact that she was able to take care of her girls without having to decide to pay a bill or buy a pair of shoes," her mother said. "But it was time away from her girls, and she had a close bond with them."

Brittanie enrolled in college and found work as a dental assistant. But the pay in Detroit was nearly double that in New Orleans, so in 2019 she struck out on her own.

"She was a go-getter. She didn't care what kind of work it was," Zelia said.

cases.name: Jaquoya Katyara "Koya" Wix
cases.about:
Her obituary said: "Jaquoya brought warmth, style, glamour, humor, and generosity into the lives of all who knew her.

Jaquoya was someone who embraced life with unmistakable spirit. She loved taking care of herself and took pride in her appearance, always making sure her makeup and hair were impeccably done. She enjoyed taking the extra time to look glamorous, and that sense of confidence and care became part of how so many will remember her. She loved taking selfies, going thrifting, and expressing herself in ways that were joyful and uniquely her own.

Music and creativity were also close to Jaquoya’s heart. She loved to sing and often used TikTok as an outlet for that joy, carefully making each video her own. Whether she was singing for one viewer or one hundred, she made sure she looked her best and gave her full self to the moment. She also loved The Gilmore Girls, happily watching episodes again and again, and she enjoyed The Temptations. In a detail that those who loved her will surely smile to remember, she liked the Chicago Bulls simply because she loved the color red in their uniforms.

Jaquoya was an excellent cook who worked at Chipotle Mexican Grill in Downtown Detroit. She loved her job, and her customers loved her in return. Her care for others could be felt not only in her work, but in the way she lived every day. She was the kind of person who would give you the shirt off her back, always looking after the people around her with a generous and giving heart.

She was also proud of her heritage and cultural identity. Jaquoya was a Native American Woman’s Traditional Dancer, and she was a member of the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians as well as the Walpole Island First Nation. These connections were a meaningful part of her life and who she was.

Above all, Jaquoya will be remembered for the love she shared with her family."
